name: O'du
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.
catalog_citation: Vy Thị Bích Thuỷ. 2016. Ngôn ngữ người Ơ Đu ở Tương Dương [The language of the Ơ Đu of Tương Dương]. Văn hóa Nghệ thuật (ISSN 0866-8655) 384 (tháng 6-2016): 32-34.

new_statements.translation: As for language, like the other ethnic groups the Ơ Đu have a language of their own; Ơ Đu belongs to the Mon-Khmer languages, and a certain proportion of its basic vocabulary carries Việt-Mường elements. 'This is an archaic language that still preserves many initial consonant clusters, sometimes triple ones, such as bnt, đrb, hem, phrv, thrm... Here tone, too, has already begun to emerge (is incipient), although the contrasting word pairs are not yet numerous. The Ơ Đu today usually communicate with one another in several languages: Vietnamese, Thái, Khơ Mú' (3). [note 3 = Đặng Nghiêm Vạn 1978, p. 115]

new_statements.relation_note: Second-hand: the article quotes verbatim Đặng Nghiêm Vạn's 1978 ethnographic profile (p.115) saying Ơ Đu keeps many initial clusters and that tone is incipient ('đã manh nha') with few contrasting pairs. Nothing on word stress/accent anywhere in the article. The rest is sociolinguistic: c. 5 elderly semi-speakers at Văng Môn; a 232-word district teaching list with 40 Thai and 28 Vietnamese loans; Vietnamese loans adapted 'chỉ thay đổi thanh điệu hoặc biến âm' (only changing the tone or altering sounds) to Ơ Đu pronunciation.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone is nascent/marginal in Ơ Đu: some tonal contrasts exist but minimal pairs are few (per Đặng Nghiêm Vạn 1978 as quoted); no statement about the position or existence of word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the tonal contrast is said to be limited ('các cặp từ đối lập chưa nhiều')
new_statements.identity_note: Explicitly the Ơ Đu (tyh) of Văng Môn/Nga My and formerly Kim Đa, Kim Tiến, Tương Dương district, Nghệ An; language described as Môn-Khơme; matches oduu1239 (Vietnamese variety).

new_statements.translation: … [compared with] the tones of Vietnamese, the Ơ Đu language has a level tone (bằng), a falling ('slanting-down') tone like the nặng tone, a rising ('slanting-up') tone like the sắc tone, and a low level tone like the huyền tone. There may also be a tone rather like the hỏi tone. The number of contrasting (minimal) pairs is in fact not large, and most of these pairs involve words borrowed from other peoples … [examples:] blung 'village' / phróm 'thin' / blúng 'fat' / droong 'gaze, look' / doong 'word denoting female' …

new_statements.relation_note: Tone inventory by analogy with Vietnamese tones; few minimal pairs; initial clusters incl. triple clusters elsewhere in the essay (per the 1978 condensation). No stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ơ Đu is described as having (incipient) lexical tone: four tones likened to Vietnamese ngang, nặng, sắc and huyền, possibly a fifth hỏi-like tone; tonal minimal pairs are few and mostly involve loanwords. Nothing is said about word stress/accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Author himself qualifies the claim: few minimal pairs, most involving loans from neighbouring languages (Thái, Khơ Mú); the hỏi-like tone is uncertain ('có thể').
new_statements.identity_note: Ethnographic sketch of the Ơ Đu (autonym phrom Ơ Đu, exonym Tày Hạt) of Tương Dương, Nghệ An by the ethnologist who did the 1970s fieldwork; language section describes Ơ Đu as Môn-Khơme with initial clusters and gives the tone remarks quoted. This is the first-hand source behind the second-hand 1978 profile quoted by Vy 2016 (pass-1 statement) — the 1973 article is fuller (names the tones and gives minimal pairs). Not in Cheeseman, Sidwell & Osborne 2017, not in Glottolog; cited in Proschan 1996's reference list and throughout the Nghệ An regional literature. | Regional folk-culture gazetteer of Nghệ An–Hà Tĩnh; the Ơ-đu (Tày Hạt) of Tương Dương/Kỳ Sơn = O'du [tyh]. Second-hand: the language paragraph condenses Đặng Nghiêm Vạn 1973 (listed in its bibliography), using the same example pairs. | Comparative paper whose subject is Kháng [kjm]; Ơ Đu [tyh] appears as one of the compared Khmuic languages with cited forms (e.g. 'Ơ Đu ro? ruiʼih drdeen') and in the concluding classification remarks ('vị trí của tiếng Mal, Ơ Đu …'). The tone remark is a statement about all Khmuic members, hence covers Ơ Đu only implicitly. Plausibly by Tạ Quang Tùng (the institute's Kháng/Khmuic phonetician, cf. pass-1 pointer Tùng 2017b) — authorship NOT verified. | The paper's subject is Khmu register/tone; the two Iduh passages are comparative asides but FIRST-HAND: the author is the Mahidol linguist who located Iduh and compiled the c. 2000-word Iduh list 'with initial phonological analysis' (our list of works to obtain Premsrirat 2005); she identifies it as 'Iduh, a Khmuic language spoken in the same area as the Khmu in Laos and Vietnam' = O'du [tyh]. Not listed for O'du by Glottolog or by Cheeseman, Sidwell & Osborne 2017. | Comparative Austroasiatic chapter; 'Khmuic (Iduh)' = O'du. new_statements.quote: In this dialect, the word with voiced initial consonant in Dia 1 has become a word with lower pitch and lax/breathy voice quality whereas the word with voiceless initial consonant in Dia 1 has higher pitch and clear tense voice quality as shown in the first column of table 2. Even though the lax register here does not have the strong breathy voice quality as in other Mon-Khmer languages such as Mon, Chong, Kuy or Iduh but it is quite distinctive for the native speakers. [...] The correct tense register especially in a variety of Khmu Khroang spoken in Chiengrai is very loud and tense. I guess that if the environment allows this sound may be developed into a creaky voice quality as shown in Iduh, a Khmuic language spoken in the same area as the Khmu in Laos and Vietnam. However my informant told me that very often, especially in front of outsiders, they do not make the correct harsh and tense voice because they do not want to be different from Thai speakers.
new_statements.citation: Suwilai Premsrirat. 2001. Tonogenesis in Khmu dialects of SEA. In Graham W. Thurgood (ed.), Papers from the Ninth Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (1999), 121-134. Tempe: Arizona State University, Program for Southeast Asian Studies. [also printed as Mon-Khmer Studies 31: 47-56 (2001); further developed as 'Register complex and tonogenesis in Khmu dialects', MKS 34: 1-17 (2004)]
new_statements.locator: p. 128 (PDF page 8 of the SALA file), section on Western Khmu with register contrast (Dia 2.1); text from scanned (tesseract eng, 150 dpi) of the scanned page, read in context pp. 127-129.
new_statements.relation_note: Iduh has a strongly breathy lax register and a creaky/tense register (register language); no tone inventory claimed; no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Iduh (O'du) is characterised by the linguist who recorded it as a REGISTER (phonation) language: a lax register with strong breathy voice (grouped with Mon, Chong, Kuy) and a tense register realised with creaky ('harsh and tense') voice. No claim of lexical pitch-tone and nothing on word stress; recorded under statement_type 'tone' as the tone-adjacent prosodic category (register), reading 'unclear or contradictory' because it is neither a stress nor a tone-inventory statement and it conflicts with Đặng Nghiêm Vạn's 'four tones' impression (A work 1).
new_statements.exceptions: none for Iduh (the remark about suppressing the tense voice 'in front of outsiders' concerns her Khmu informants)

sources.quote: Về ngôn ngữ, cũng như các dân tộc khác, người Ơ đu có ngôn ngữ riêng, tiếng Ơ đu thuộc ngôn ngữ Môn - Khơme, trong các từ vị cơ bản có một tỷ lệ nhất định mang yếu tố Việt Mường. “Đây là một thứ tiếng cổ còn giữ được nhiều phụ âm đầu kép, có khi cặp ba như: bnt, đrb, hem, phrv, thrm... Ở đây thanh điệu cũng đã manh nha, mặc dầu các cặp từ đối lập chưa nhiều. Người Ơ đu ngày nay thường giao tiếp với nhau bằng nhiều thứ tiếng: tiếng phổ thông, tiếng Thái, tiếng Khơ mú” (3). [note 3: Đặng Nghiêm Vạn, Các dân tộc ít người Việt Nam, Nxb Khoa học Xã hội, Hà Nội, 1978, tr. 115]
sources.locator: p. 32 (right column), with endnote 3 on p. 34 citing Đặng Nghiêm Vạn 1978: 115
sources.note: Second-hand: the article quotes verbatim Đặng Nghiêm Vạn's 1978 ethnographic profile (p.115) saying Ơ Đu keeps many initial clusters and that tone is incipient ('đã manh nha') with few contrasting pairs. Nothing on word stress/accent anywhere in the article. The rest is sociolinguistic: c. 5 elderly semi-speakers at Văng Môn; a 232-word district teaching list with 40 Thai and 28 Vietnamese loans; Vietnamese loans adapted 'chỉ thay đổi thanh điệu hoặc biến âm' (only changing the tone or altering sounds) to Ơ Đu pronunciation.

Nhìn lại những hiện tượng vừa nêu, một lần nữa chúng ta lại thấy, ngay ở lĩnh vực ngữ âm, sự cách tân của các thành viên được so [sánh] … / … việc xếp tiếng Kháng vào nhánh Khmuic với các ngôn ngữ Khabit, Khơ Mú, Xinh Mun là hoàn toàn hợp lí. sources.citation: Suwilai Premsrirat. 2001. Tonogenesis in Khmu dialects of SEA. In Graham W. Thurgood (ed.), Papers from the Ninth Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (1999), 121-134. Tempe: Arizona State University, Program for Southeast Asian Studies. [also printed as Mon-Khmer Studies 31: 47-56 (2001); further developed as 'Register complex and tonogenesis in Khmu dialects', MKS 34: 1-17 (2004)]
sources.quote: In this dialect, the word with voiced initial consonant in Dia 1 has become a word with lower pitch and lax/breathy voice quality whereas the word with voiceless initial consonant in Dia 1 has higher pitch and clear tense voice quality as shown in the first column of table 2. Even though the lax register here does not have the strong breathy voice quality as in other Mon-Khmer languages such as Mon, Chong, Kuy or Iduh but it is quite distinctive for the native speakers. [...] The correct tense register especially in a variety of Khmu Khroang spoken in Chiengrai is very loud and tense. I guess that if the environment allows this sound may be developed into a creaky voice quality as shown in Iduh, a Khmuic language spoken in the same area as the Khmu in Laos and Vietnam. However my informant told me that very often, especially in front of outsiders, they do not make the correct harsh and tense voice because they do not want to be different from Thai speakers.
sources.locator: p. 128 (PDF page 8 of the SALA file), section on Western Khmu with register contrast (Dia 2.1); text from scanned (tesseract eng, 150 dpi) of the scanned page, read in context pp. 127-129.
sources.note: Iduh has a strongly breathy lax register and a creaky/tense register (register language); no tone inventory claimed; no stress statement.
